2392.dq: The stress accent is distinctive on the morphological level only, e.g. be'še 'he went', 'beše 'go!'. (p.278)
2392.dloc: p.278 (Phonology, after Vowels: the stress sentence); p.279 n.2 (stressed lexical -a vs unstressed Fem. -a); p.282 (Verb: stressed/unstressed prefixes; n.5); p.283 (preterite stem-final stress; imperfect = preterite with m(e)-; perfect participle final vowel stressed; passive participle -is'ta); p.277 (phonetic transcriptions)., (leaf = page+20).
2392.prule: No general word-stress position is stated. The only general sentence says stress contrasts are morphological, not lexical ('distinctive on the morphological level only'): the imperative and present-subjunctive prefix b(e)- is stressed ('beše 'go!', 'be-žan 'hit!'); the present-indicative and imperfect prefix m(e)-, the conditional prefix b(e)- and the preterite prefix b(e)- are unstressed, the preterite (and the imperfect, which behaves like it) carrying stress on the last syllable of the stem (be'še 'he went', bevritim, bebeym); the perfect and pluperfect stress the final vowel of the past participle (āhar'de, bi'a, har'da-m); the passive-participle suffix -is'ta is stressed; the feminine direct-case ending -a is unstressed while lexical final -a is stressed (suka'la, xaso'ra). Position is thus set by affix identity/tense category over a stem-final locus. The author's transcriptions (p.277) mark every bare nominal stem-finally (kɪl'lɪg, hoṷ'lɪg, xæso'rɪg, zæl'lɪk, ɪn'dʒɑ; enclitic -em unstressed in zə'negəm), so a stem-final default is inferable but is not stated as a rule.

2394.heavy: 'слоги закрытого типа' (closed-type syllables) in disyllables attract stress to the second syllable; open-syllable disyllables take initial stress. Long vowels (Karatsan govor only) are secondary contractions 'не имеют фонологической значимости' and play no role in stress.
2394.dflt: initial in open-syllable disyllables; second syllable in trisyllables; lexically listed exceptions (уршú, уццú, риццú, умрá, диснá, чиркá, дярхя́ final-stressed open disyllables); no data for 4+ syllables
2394.prule: Stress is 'clearly expressed, of varying position (разноместное) and mobile (подвижное)', in explicit contrast with literary Dargwa; it is phonologically distinctive (minimal pairs in segmentally identical forms: бáрив 'did' / барúв 'done'; дугьа 'front room' / дугьа 'in the front room'; бáра 'do!' / барá 'a little'; 2025 adds дýли 'I.ERG' / дулú 'pus', дýгъа/дугъá, бáлкIа/балкIá and states 'Ударным может быть любой слог' = any syllable may be stressed). Positional tendencies stated by syllable count and syllable type: disyllables of open syllables -> first syllable; disyllables with closed-type syllables and trisyllables -> second syllable; morphology overrides these (plural formants, negative/prohibitive particles, preverbs in converbs, adjectival -кан stressed, -ци pre-stressing). The 2025 restatement hedges the positional rules ('как правило', 'обычно') and lists lexical exceptions in both directions. No word longer than three syllables is covered by a rule.

Il est évident que l'orthographe kakɔ doit tenir compte de ces faits par des signes tonals (orthographe tonale). [...] Sur la base de notre analyse du système tonal de l'énoncé associ…

2395.tone: Two-tone (H/L) system. Ernst 1992:14-16: two distinctive tones haut and bas, at least six phonetic pitch levels, tones 'ponctuels' vs 'modulés' (rising/falling), only low tone marked in the orthography; p.27: the vowel bearing a contour tone is longer, long vowels arise from grammatical processes. Ernst 1991 (Description tonologique, p.33): 'Toute voyelle est porteuse d'un ton ponctuel, soit haut, soit bas'; p.34: two distinctive tones, a property of the syllable, no tone-bearing syllabic consonants. Ernst 1995: mid = downstepped H, contour tones in verb forms. Yukawa 1992: H, rising, falling marks, unmarked = L, verbs in tonal groups A/B/C. None of these texts contains any word-stress / accent d'intensité statement: a letter-spacing-tolerant regex over all held (accent, intensit, stress, tonique, proémin, prominen, penult, allong) finds 'accent' only as accent grave/aigu/circonflexe (tone diacritics) and 'mettre l'accent sur' (emphasis), and 'stress' only inside 'les astres sont'.

2401.prule: Non-contrastive word stress confined to the first two syllables; default initial. 2402.dq: Every Kambaata word has one and generally only one prominent, stressed syllable – with the exception of words that host case-marked enclitics, which may carry two stresses, one on the host and one on the enclitic. 2402.prule: One stressed syllable per word, its position assigned by the inflectional morphology, not by syllable count or weight: roots and derivational suffixes are stressless; every inflectional suffix (case/gender on nouns and adjectives, the subject-aspect/mood/dependency complex on verbs) carries a stress specification (suprafix) realized (a) on the suffix itself, (b) on the syllable preceding it, (c) on the pre-preceding syllable, (d) on the syllable following it, or (e) at the right edge of the word; e.g. F.NOM -´a > lókkanne 'our feet', F.ACC -á > lokkánne, F.GEN -a´# > lokkanné 'of our feet'; post-inflectional suffixes are stress-neutral or stress-changing (COP1 -_´ta, jussive negator -´ka, relative suprafix -´#).
2402.srule: None: 'Every Kambaata word has one and generally only one prominent, stressed syllable [...] Words of one (3) up to eleven syllables (4) are attested in Kambaata with only one prominent syllable.' 2407.heavy: Three-degree scale taken over from the Hindi analyses (Pandey 1989, Dyrud 2001, Hussain 1997), which Eaton says Kangri follows in most details: 'monomoraic or LIGHT (i.e. CV), bimoraic or HEAVY (i.e. CVC or CVV), and trimoraic or SUPERHEAVY (i.e. CVVC or CVCC). The weight is based on the rhyme of the syllable only; onsets are irrelevant... the vowels [i, e, æ, u, o, ɔ, ɑ] are bimoraic, while the vowels [ɪ, ʊ, ə] count as a single mora' (pp. 50-51). The word-final mora is extrametrical (sec. 4.3.4). Underlying /ɦ/ (which surfaces as tone) still counts as a coda consonant for weight at the time stress is assigned (exx. 19-20, pp. 63-64).
2407.dflt: First syllable of the stem (sec. 4.3.2, Table 4-2: 'If All Syllables are LIGHT, then Stress the First Syllable'). Fn. 31 (p. 56) gives the author's opinion that words whose syllables all have equal weight 'effectively' have no primary stress and that the observed initial stress may be a citation-form elicitation effect (M. Ohala 1977 found penultimate stress for Hindi in a sentence frame).
2407.prule: Within the stem only (root plus derivational affixes; inflectional affixes are invisible), and with the word-final mora extrametrical, stress the heaviest syllable; if several syllables tie as heaviest, stress the right-most of them; if all stem syllables are light, stress the first syllable. Unbounded (no window) within the stem.

tn.quote: Kangri behaves more like an accentual language. Kangri has one level tone and two contour tones. The level tone is overwhelmingly the default tone for Kangri syllables. … even when a word has a contour tone in it, the tone always occurs on the stressed syllable. The fact that there are only a few tones that are both sparsely distributed and tied to a specific (stressed) syllable suggests that Kangri fits the pattern of an accentual language. … S. L. Sharma (1974), Chauhan (1992), S. R. Sharma (1998), all describe Kangri as having 3 tones: high-falling, low-rising, and level.

tn.note: Three tones: default level plus high-falling and low-rising contours, found only on the weight-stressed syllable; analysed as accentual: contour = H on stressed syllable + L from underlying /ɦ/.

2408.dq: Minimal word pairs contrast as to the syllables on which the tone is placed. ... In KANITE also, high tone and stress always occur on the same syllable.
2408.prule: No positional stress rule. The single contrastive suprasegmental of Kanite is a lexically placed high tone (vs. low/toneless syllables), shown by minimal pairs differing only in which syllable(s) carry the tone (ke'na 'skirt' vs 'ke'na 'bamboo'); stress (intensity) is stated to fall always on the high-toned syllable, so stress is a concomitant of tone, not an independent or predictable position.
2408.srule: Not mentioned in Young 1962, Sec. 3.3 'Supra-segmental Phonemes', pp. 98-99: for Kanite Young states only that 'high tone and stress always occur on the same syllable'; a second (Kamano) or light (Benabena) stress is described there for those two stress languages only. The Gibson & McCarthy OPD (1992) p. 3 ('Stress occurs on high tone. Kanite has two phonemic tones.') likewise does not discuss secondary stress.
2408.quote: In these four languages the contrastive supra-segmental feature is not so much one of pitch levels or stress intensity as of syllable emphasis. That is, each language has one distinct supra-segmental phoneme which when it occurs gives contrast to affected syllables over neutral syllables. In KANITE and GAHUKU it is a phoneme of tone, which has been described as high tone and which contrasts with syllables which may be described as being either low tone or toneless. Minimal word pairs contrast as to the syllables on which the tone is placed. Examples: ... KANITE ke'na "skirt" 'ke'na "bamboo" .…
2408.idn: Kanite (Young: 'KANITE'; OPD: 'Kanite (Kemeyu Kanite) [KMU]'); data: Young 1962 excerpt: not stated in held pages. Gibson & McCarthy: a Kanite village, Eastern Highlands (Okapa), residence April 1957 - July 1967; OPD data checked April 1992, villages Kemeyu, Anupalu, Ko'kopi, Kuana.
2408.exq_: in KANITE there are no toneless (completely low tone) words, the only examples being nouns which form part of a compound verb expression and which are therefore bound to the verb stem.
2408.tone: Young 1962 (p. 98): Kanite (like Gahuku) has 'a phoneme of tone, which has been described as high tone and which contrasts with syllables which may be described as being either low tone or toneless'; minimal word pairs differ only in tone placement; (p. 99) tone occurs on nouns and verbs, there are no toneless words except nouns bound into compound verb expressions, noun tone is perturbed by a preceding adjective (by adjective class and the vowel of the noun's initial syllable) but not between adjacent nouns and verbs; 'high tone and stress always occur on the same syllable'. Corroborated in the held SIL Organised Phonology Data for Kanite (Kemeyu Kanite) [KMU], data checked Gibson/McCarthy April 1992, printed 2004, p. 3 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)': 'Stress occurs on high tone. Kanite has two phonemic tones.' and 'Tone is not written.' (publisher-text). McCarthy 1965 footnote, reprinted in the Gibson & McCarthy grammar sketch (scan of p. 115): 'Stress is phonemic but carries a low functional load. It is marked in only one part of the paper where it signals the difference in a minimal pair'. No source gives a positional or weight rule for stress; stress is wholly parasitic on lexical high tone.

2412.dq: The marking of the primary stress, however, is determined by the length or the number of syllables a word has. [...] When words receive affixes (or enter into compounds), the resulting longer form still maintains stress on the root.
2412.dloc: Ch. 2 'Phonology', sec. 2.2.1 'Stress', thesis pp. 40-42; pp. 41-42 also checked as rendered for the diacritics.
2412.prule: Primary stress on the final syllable of disyllabic words and on the penultimate syllable of words of three or more syllables; syllable count = vowel count, except that the diphthongs ai, ei, ou count as one syllable. The position is computed on the root: affixed and compounded forms keep the root's stress (àmára-bogɨ, ɸòxú-ogu), so within a suffixed word the primary stress need not be final/penultimate of the whole word. quantity-insensitive; no reference to vowel length or codas.
2412.srule: Secondary stress on the first syllable of every word, regardless of length or syllable count (tì, tògai, sòganɨ, kɨ̀meyiaru, tàitsambra); one secondary per word, so disyllables carry initial secondary + final primary (tòxú) and longer words initial secondary + penultimate primary (sògánɨ, kàdibóxu, kàsarédsai). No alternating stresses described.
2412.quote: Stress is not phonemically contrastive in Sare and is partially predictable in that stress rules depend on a division of the word into syllables. 2415.prule: Main (dynamic, force) word stress on the final syllable of the word; the source calls it 'bound, fixed, single-place' (связанное, фиксированное, одноместное) and mobile in the sense that it moves rightward onto each added suffix (ада́м – адамла́ – адамлары́ – адамларыбы́з – адамларыбызґа́). Weight plays no role: stress is described as purely dynamic, with no quantitative or musical component (contrasted explicitly with Yakut, Kirghiz, Turkmen and with Turkish/Uzbek). The rule is hedged ('обычно падает на последний слог') and the source lists many non-final classes (see exceptions).
2415.srule: Secondary stress on the first syllable of words of four or more syllables (main stress on the final syllable): ѝшлериклé 'those who will work', àшарыкъланы̀ 'that which is to be eaten'. In compounds and reduplications the component without the main stress carries a secondary stress on its last syllable: қара́ нанық (main stress on the last syllable of the first component, secondary on the last syllable of the second), қара̀дура́, қалґа̀нбулґа́н (main stress word-final, secondary on the last syllable of the first component).

conflict.would_settle: The sides describe different dialects thirty-odd years apart (side 1: Nangu, Bidyadanga 1992; side 2: coastal Najanaja, Beagle Bay Mission informants, pre-1962), so both may be true of their own variety; what is unsettled is the language-level primary position in words of 4+ syllables. It would be settled by the unread modern grammar of Capell's own dialect, Sharp, Janet. 2004. 'A Grammar of Najanaja Karajarri', RCLT La Trobe draft, 392 pp. (bibliography row 11, Glottolog 553637, access class unknown: not located online or in the libraries checked; Glottolog/HH list a private scan): if its phonology chapter reports initial primary stress with alternating secondaries in long words, Capell's penult 'main stress' is a ranking/phrase-prominence artefact and the record resolves to fixed-initial (rule strings 10 100 1000 10000..., secondary optional on odd syllables); if it reports penultimate primary in words of four or more syllables, the record is fixed with a length-dependent position (10 100 1010 10010-type strings) at least for Najanaja, with a possible Nangu/Najanaja split. Second-best: Sands 1989 'A Grammar of Garadjari' (ANU Hons, Najanaja from Laves' 1929-31 texts; AIATSIS MS 2863 closed, MPI-EVA PL 7101.G2 SAN 1989; listed link dead) and McKelson's Karajarri sketch (McGregor ed. 1996 Coate Festschrift, print only). An instrumental comparison of four- and five-syllable words in isolation vs phrase-final position would also decide it.

deciding.quote: No detailed study of stress has been done in Karajarri, but as is typical of most Australian languages, basic stress patterns can be described by the following principles (Dixon, 1980): primary stress occurs on the initial syllable of a word, and secondary stress sometimes (though less common in rapid speech) on the third, fifth etc. syllables. A typical sentence form one of the texts, for example, has roughly the following stress pattern (this sentence is from text A.1.1): yánu pála jálangkà…

2417.cfw: Johnson 1992 (Nangu dialect) describes primary stress on the initial syllable with secondary stress on alternate syllables and Thieberger 1993 says the same for the region generally, but Capell 1962 (coastal Najanaja dialect) places main stress on the penultimate syllable in words of four or more syllables (ˌgali'guru 'boomerang') while agreeing on initial stress in two- and three-syllable words, and since Johnson himself notes that no detailed study of Karajarri stress has been made, initial stress is the likely reading but its placement in longer words is unsettled.
